newSounds: Korean has no tones, so pitch never changes a word's meaning. The real work is a three-way consonant contrast: plain g/d/b/j/s are unaspirated (like the k in 'skate'), aspirated k/t/p/ch carry a puff of air (like Telugu ఖ/థ/ఫ), and tense kk/tt/pp/ss/jj are clipped and hard with no puff. r/l is a light flap like Telugu ర; eu is like the i in 'cousin' and has no clean Telugu match; ae and e are both about eh, and oe and we are both about weh. ng is silent at the start of a syllable but sounds like ng at the end.
rhythm: Syllable-timed: each block is one even beat, close to Telugu syllable rhythm. Seoul Korean has no strong lexical stress, so the voice only leans a little harder on the phrase-final syllable; that is where CAPS is placed in youSay. Keep beats even and unhurried.
registerFirst: Polite first. ~yo closes everyday polite sentences; ~seumnida / ~seumnikka are the formal versions for strangers, elders and officials. The honorific infix -si- and the humble je instead of na raise the listener; casual ~hae / ~ya are for friends and family only. Titles and kinship terms often replace 'you'.
trap: Batchim (final consonants) are the big trap: they are unreleased — final k, t and p are stopped, not exploded — and they change at boundaries. gamsahamnida is said gam-sah-ham-ni-da (b turns into m before n), geot+eun becomes i-ge-seun, and l+n merges to ll (il-nyeon -> il-lyeon). Do not mix tense and aspirated sounds: kk is not k, tt is not t, pp is not p, ss is not s. Finally, s before i or a y-vowel sounds like sh.
